column4: Trained hunting animals are taught what to catch for their keeper. Their learned obedience gives a concrete counterpart to the source's tamed animal that follows a leader and serves an owner.

It asks whether the One who guides to truth is more worthy of being followed than one who cannot guide unless guided. This gives the source's hâdî and following herd an explicit criterion for a true leader.

God makes paths through the earth, sends down water, and brings out paired plants; 20:54 then tells people to pasture their livestock. This ayah supplies the route and growth that make the next ayah's grazing possible.
After 24:45 differentiates animal movement, this ayah says God guides whom He wills to a straight path. It joins creaturely motion to the section's requested direction without conflating the two.
God brings out the earth's water and pasture; 79:33 identifies that created order as provision for people and their cattle. This ayah contributes the grazing ground itself.
God creates and proportionates; 87:3 then says He determines and guides. The ayah contributes the making-fit side of the source's guide-and-creature image.
Those who follow the messenger, support him, and follow the light sent down with him are called successful. It gives the source's following relation a revealed guide and a communal response.
People are commanded to believe in the messenger and follow him so that they may be guided. It directly joins following a leader to receiving guidance.
Among the created are a community that guides by truth and acts justly by it. This supplies a collective form of reliable guidance rather than a lone animal leader.
Following 12:39's rival masters, Joseph says judgment belongs only to God and that people are commanded to worship Him alone. It gives the source's owner-and-service relation its exclusive object.
The Prophet calls to God with insight, “I and whoever follows me.” The ayah makes a guided way a visible chain of leader and followers.
After calling the Prophet a warner, it says that every people has a guide. The source's hâdî is thereby widened from a herd's front animal to a people-specific guide.
All moving creatures in the heavens and earth prostrate to God. The source's `na'budu` and tamed-animal relation meet in creatures whose submission belongs to their maker.
Moses and Aaron are told to announce peace for whoever follows guidance. It attaches a concrete promised outcome to the source's act of following the guide.
In the sacrificial-rites passage, benefits remain in the offerings until an appointed term, then their destination is the Ancient House. It adds duration and destination to the animal scene of 22:36.
Birds in flight each know their own prayer and glorification. An animal collective has an ordered response to its Lord, extending the source's herd-under-owner image without making birds livestock.
An ant warns its community to enter their dwellings before Solomon's forces arrive. Like the source's bee and herd details, it stages an animal community receiving a protective lead from within.
God creates and disperses living creatures through the heavens and earth, and can gather them when He wills. The wild herd's apparent freedom is set inside a larger divine power to gather.
Pharaoh makes his people compliant and they obey him. It is a false human herd-leader: obedience follows a deceiving ruler rather than a trustworthy guide.

The simile describes a recipient hearing only a call and cry. Its animal referent is implicit rather than named, so it only tentatively parallels a herd that must recognize its caller rather than hear meaningless noise.
The ayah notices varied colors among beasts and livestock. It offers an indirect natural counterpart to the source's visible identifying mark, though color here is not an ownership brand.
